lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on what the law should punish
lead.head: No victim, no crime

pic.caption: Ajay Shah (left) and Amit Varma early in Episode 73

play.label: Hear the case in six steps

body: Someone wrote in after an ear­lier episode with a ques­tion: what is a vic­tim­less crime? Doesn’t every crime have a vic­tim?

Amit Varma’s an­swer, over the next hour, was that the phrase is a mis­nomer. A crime, he said, in­fringes someone’s rights: killing them, or steal­ing their prop­erty. Acts that harm no one are not crimes at all. “If there is a crime, there must be a vic­tim.” {073-C01}
Being il­le­gal, he ar­gued, is not the same as being wrong. Most such laws come from a wish not merely to pro­tect rights but to “en­gi­neer so­ci­ety to our wishes”.
Varma, with Ajay Shah ask­ing the ques­tions, took the idea through al­co­hol, drugs, gam­bling, pros­ti­tu­tion, ho­mo­sex­u­al­ity, sui­cide and hate speech.
## Three ob­jec­tions

His case rested on three ob­jec­tions. The first is moral: con­sent­ing adults should be free to as­so­ciate with each other as they please, “whether it is in the bed­room, the mar­ket­place, or the pub­lic square”.
The sec­ond is prac­ti­cal. A ban does not end de­mand: the un­der­world springs up, co­er­cion and fraud come in, and the de­sired out­come never ar­rives.

The third is about power. Whoever holds the state’s mo­nop­oly on co­er­cion will use it to re­make so­ci­ety to their own val­ues. “The per­son you hate most in the world could be in power to­mor­row,” Varma warned, “and they’ll pass laws ac­cord­ing to their val­ues.” {073-C02}

Prohibition was the clear­est case. Drawing on the reg­u­la­tory econ­o­mist Bruce Yandle, Varma de­scribed two ap­par­ent en­e­mies: the Baptist, who de­mands a ban on moral grounds, and the boot­leg­ger, who prof­its from it.
“The Baptist wants al­co­hol banned, so he can do his virtue sig­nal­ing,” he said, “and the boot­leg­ger wants al­co­hol banned so he can make money on the black mar­ket.” {073-C03}

Wherever the state bans some­thing, the po­lice also find lever­age. Varma’s stark­est ex­am­ple was the Matunga racket, in which Bombay po­lice posed as men look­ing for love to trap and ex­tort gay men.
## Instinct and rea­son
Not every case was sim­ple. Varma told of a German can­ni­bal whose vic­tim con­sented on cam­era, and of thought ex­per­i­ments that in­stinct con­demns but rea­son can­not fault.

Moral in­stincts, he said, come from pre­his­toric pro­gram­ming no­body fully un­der­stands. When the pow­er­ful want to out­law some­thing be­cause it feels wrong, that is all the more rea­son for sus­pi­cion.
Shah added that even the rich­est states ex­e­cute in­no­cent peo­ple, and India has very lit­tle state ca­pa­bil­ity to spare.
## Means and ends

If the worry is wives beaten by drunk hus­bands, Shah ar­gued, ban­ning al­co­hol is the wrong lever. The right one is easy no-fault di­vorce, with jointly cre­ated wealth split equally, so that an abused spouse can walk away.
“So just an emo­tional out­rage is the surest way of get­ting to a wrong an­swer,” he said. {073-C15}
Growth, Shah added, is the great­est in­stru­ment for the eman­ci­pa­tion of women. Varma ex­tended that to every marginalised group.

Shah closed with Alan Turing, whose life was de­stroyed by British laws on ho­mo­sex­u­al­ity. The main­stream was once com­pletely wrong about ho­mo­sex­u­al­ity and di­vorce, he said, and get­ting the state out worked.
Once you ac­cept that, Shah said, you should doubt the rest of con­ven­tional wis­dom on state power, drug laws in­cluded. {073-C17}
Varma’s last word was a prin­ci­ple: the co­er­cive power of the state should never get in the way of in­di­vid­u­als, “even if you re­gard their ac­tions as un­eth­i­cal”.

second.label: Criminal justice
second.head: The state’s fatal errors
second.deck: Ajay Shah on the death penalty, and what it says about state power

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the death penalty’s error rate

body: Roughly 5 per cent of peo­ple ex­e­cuted by the state in ad­vanced economies are later be­lieved to have been in­no­cent, Ajay Shah said. These are coun­tries with the best state ca­pa­bil­ity in the world, whose judges de­mand the high­est level of ev­i­dence. {073-C13}

“Under Indian con­di­tions,” he asked, “what do you think is the fail rate of the state?” He had no es­ti­mates, but large num­bers of in­no­cent peo­ple, he said, are put into the slam­mer by the Indian state. {#slammer}
Every con­vic­tion, Shah ar­gued, de­serves scep­ti­cism, and so does any plan to turn such a flawed in­stru­ment on people’s pri­vate choices.

quote.text: One in twenty is ac­tu­ally in­no­cent, and the state went and caught the wrong guy or did some hor­ri­ble things.

third.head: Beautiful intent, bad law

pic.caption: Amit Varma on the MP and the hate-speech bill

body: At a lit­er­ary fes­ti­val re­cently, Amit Varma shared a stage with an MP who had brought a bill against hate speech on plat­forms. “I get the in­tent,” Varma told him. “It’s very beau­ti­ful.” {073-S06}

Then came the warn­ing, from twenty-five years of writ­ing about free speech: “Laws against hate speech will al­ways be used against free speech.” Always and ev­ery­where, he said, the state uses such laws to at­tack dis­senters. {073-C11}
Varma, a free speech ab­so­lutist, draws the line at di­rect in­cite­ment to harm: telling some­one to go and beat Amit is wrong be­cause the beat­ing is a crime.
Laws such as 295A and 153A sound well meant, but can be read to lock up any­one. Hate speech is bad, he said, but power over it will be turned on “peo­ple like us”.

p2.title: Mind your own business
p2.deck: Amit Varma takes his case against punishing victimless crimes through alcohol, gambling and the limits of the state

quote.text: We should not au­to­mat­i­cally as­sume that what­ever is il­le­gal is nec­es­sar­ily wrong from an eth­i­cal per­spec­tive

photo.caption: John Locke in 1697, painted by Sir Godfrey Kneller

box.title: The right behind the rights
box.text: All of mod­ern lib­er­al­ism, Amit Varma said, em­anates from John Locke’s idea of self-ownership. “I am my own prop­erty, I own my­self.” The rights to life, free speech and prop­erty all flow from that. {#locke}

sections.label: The principle
sections.head: Illegal, but not wrong
sections.caption: the line between illegal and wrong
body: In the pop­u­lar imag­i­na­tion, Amit Varma said, break­ing the law is a crime. That is legally cor­rect. The larger ques­tion is what the law should con­sider a crime, and what­ever is il­le­gal is not nec­es­sar­ily wrong. {#illegal}

His own test is a lib­eral one. All of us have rights, and they hold only as far as they do not in­fringe the rights of oth­ers. Murder in­fringes the right to life, theft the right to prop­erty, and the whole pur­pose of the state is to stop such in­fringe­ments.

Victimless crimes harm no one else. The state out­laws them any­way, he ar­gued, be­cause it wants to re­make so­ci­ety, tweak­ing laws “like an en­gi­neer does” until it gets the out­comes it de­sires.
## The case against bans

The first of his ob­jec­tions is moral: when the state in­ter­feres with vol­un­tary in­ter­ac­tions that harm no one else, “ev­ery­thing goes to hell”. The sec­ond is prac­ti­cal: a ban does not end de­mand, so the un­der­world comes in and things get worse.

The third is about power. The state needs a mo­nop­oly on co­er­cion to pro­tect rights, Varma said, but it ex­ists to serve us, not the other way round. Give it power to re­fash­ion so­ci­ety, and who­ever holds it next will pass laws ac­cord­ing to their own val­ues. {073-C02}
~ Homosexuality, ef­fec­tively il­le­gal in India until re­cently, showed the cost. Those were “the mores of an ear­lier, darker time”, he said, and they de­stroyed lives.

quote.text: We should not au­to­mat­i­cally as­sume that what­ever is il­le­gal is nec­es­sar­ily wrong from an eth­i­cal per­spec­tive

sections.label: Alcohol
sections.head: The pulpit and the still
sections.caption: Baptists and bootleggers
body: Prohibition, Amit Varma said, has never worked any­where in human his­tory. He has had al­co­hol in Gujarat, and in Lahore, where de­spite pro­hi­bi­tion there was a flour­ish­ing black mar­ket. {073-S04}

He bor­rowed a frame from the reg­u­la­tory econ­o­mist Bruce Yandle. A Baptist gives moral grounds for a ban; then a boot­leg­ger sup­plies lower-quality, un­reg­u­lated al­co­hol, and sto­ries of hooch poi­son­ing fol­low. {#hooch}

That is why, Varma said, the film *Raees* got it com­pletely wrong by set­ting Shah Rukh Khan’s boot­leg­ger against a goody-goody anti-alcohol politi­cian. Their in­cen­tives are ex­actly aligned. {073-C03}
## The price of suc­cess

Ajay Shah added a twist. Successful en­force­ment shows up as a high black-market price, and high prices draw crim­i­nals in. “If you try to go after this and you even suc­ceed in the short term, you’re only stok­ing greater ef­fort and greater or­ga­ni­za­tional ca­pac­ity in the long run.” {073-C04}

Import du­ties, Varma said, pun­ish a vic­tim­less crime too: “I buy some­thing in America, I bring it here, and I sell it to a friend. And im­me­di­ately it is a crime be­cause I haven’t paid the hafta to the state.” {073-J05}

~ Where the state bans some­thing, he added, badly paid po­lice col­lect hafta from the un­der­world and from or­di­nary of­fend­ers. He called peo­ple in law en­force­ment ex­cel­lent peo­ple. “But the in­cen­tives are what they are.”

quote.text: I might not par­take of them, but other peo­ple have agency, and if they wish to do so, that’s the way it is.

sections.label: Gambling
sections.head: All of life is a bet
sections.caption: why we are all gamblers
body: Amit Varma was a pro­fes­sional poker player for five years. {#fiveyears} His first point about gam­bling was that ev­ery­one gam­bles.

Talking to a girl in a bar, mar­ry­ing, choos­ing a job, buy­ing a house or in­vest­ing in stocks: each is a bet on an in­tu­itive sense of prob­a­bil­i­ties. Even putting Pi on Ajay Shah’s lap dur­ing the shoot was a gam­ble, weigh­ing the risk of dis­rup­tion against “the oxy­tocin flood­ing through you”. {073-J03}
If gam­bling means weigh­ing prob­a­bil­i­ties and bet­ting on your best judg­ment, Varma said, then ev­ery­thing is gam­bling, and sin­gling out some forms for stigma makes no sense. {073-C07}
## Out of the shad­ows

Varma was a cricket jour­nal­ist for many years, when match-fixing was a scourge. People con­flate bet­ting and match-fixing, he said, but match-fixing hap­pens be­cause bet­ting is il­le­gal: the un­der­world runs it, and no­body looks at its money flows.

Imagine in­stead, he said, that HDFC or IDFC of­fered gam­bling ac­counts, much as a demat ac­count holds shares, with light-touch reg­u­la­tion against fraud and match-fixing. Everything would be in the open. “Sunlight is the best dis­in­fec­tant.” {073-C06}
~ Players are paid much more today, he noted, so the in­cen­tives for fix­ing have changed. But the shady deal­ing hap­pens wher­ever the un­der­world is.

quote.text: Everything we do is gam­bling and we should not nec­es­sar­ily stig­ma­tise cer­tain forms of gam­bling.

sections.label: State capability
sections.head: Few jobs, done well
sections.caption: the limits of state capability
body: Ajay Shah, draw­ing on his work with Vijay Kelkar, treats state ca­pa­bil­ity as a fi­nite bud­get. India, a poor coun­try, has very lit­tle of it. {073-C14}

Rich coun­tries such as Sweden or the UK can af­ford to splurge it. India, Shah said, has “a teensy-weensy amount of state ca­pa­bil­ity” and should spend it on a few pri­mor­dial, im­por­tant prob­lems. {073-J10}
Defence, mon­e­tary pol­icy, crim­i­nal jus­tice, fi­nan­cial reg­u­la­tion and a tax sys­tem: learn­ing these ba­sics, he said, is a jour­ney of fifty or a hun­dred years. {#fiftyhundred}
## First things first

Amit Varma agreed, and went fur­ther. The Indian state does too many things badly, he said, and vic­tim­less crimes should not be on its list at all. Except for the priv­i­leged, the rule of law does not exist in India. “Get that right first.”

For wives beaten by drunk hus­bands, Shah’s rem­edy is not pro­hi­bi­tion but easy, fric­tion­less no-fault di­vorce, with jointly cre­ated wealth split equally, giv­ing an abused spouse the power to walk away. {073-C15}

~ Varma reads ris­ing di­vorce rates as a sign of women’s em­pow­er­ment. He re­called a Twitter rant list­ing five things Ronald Reagan got wrong, “and as I was read­ing through them I re­al­ized that he got all of them right.” One was no-fault di­vorce. {073-J09}

quote.text: When you have very lit­tle ca­pa­bil­ity, the wise thing to do is to focus that ca­pa­bil­ity on a few pri­mor­dial and im­por­tant prob­lems

sections.label: The last word
sections.head: Fan the spark of doubt
sections.caption: Alan Turing and the spark of doubt
body: Ajay Shah’s rec­om­men­da­tion was a per­son and a story: Alan Turing. He played a crit­i­cal part in crack­ing the German Enigma ma­chines, Shah said, and was the first the­o­ret­i­cal com­puter sci­en­tist. {#turing}
Turing’s life was de­stroyed be­cause he fell afoul of old British laws about ho­mo­sex­u­al­ity. Study it, Shah said, and “it will re­shape your moral cal­cu­lus”.

For Amit Varma, Turing’s is the story of all ho­mo­sex­u­als for most of human his­tory. In India, he said, those who had to hide lived Thoreau’s “lives of quiet des­per­a­tion”, made worse be­cause they could not even ex­press their sex­u­al­ity. {073-J12}
## Where doubt leads

Shah sees de­crim­i­nalised ho­mo­sex­u­al­ity and no-fault di­vorce as the first stir­rings of lib­eral val­ues: places where peo­ple woke up, said “How dare you?” and got the gov­ern­ment out, with great suc­cess.
Once you ac­cept that main­stream think­ing was com­pletely wrong on these ques­tions, he said, you should ques­tion the rest, in­clud­ing the use of state power on drugs. {073-C17}
~ Varma’s prin­ci­ple is to get the state out first. Once that is done, he said, so­ci­ety hope­fully evolves.

quote.text: We owe it to our­selves to blow oxy­gen on the spark of doubt in our hearts
If some­one has cho­sen to be a pros­ti­tute, they have done so be­cause it is the best op­tion open to them and now it is up to you to con­tem­plate how bad the other op­tions must be.

p3.title: The case files
p3.deck: Four stories the hosts told, and what each says about bans

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on what a ban on love gave Bombay’s police
stories.head: Coffee at Matunga, cash at the ATM
body: Around 2007 and 2008, be­fore dat­ing apps, gay men in Bombay found each other through clas­si­fied web­sites, where peo­ple posted that they were look­ing for a lover or for friend­ship. {#matunga2007}

Amit Varma’s friend Vikram Doctor told him about a scheme the po­lice were run­ning. {073-R12} A po­lice­man would ad­ver­tise on such a site, pos­ing as some­one look­ing for love, and sug­gest meet­ing at Matunga sta­tion for cof­fee and a chat.
When the man ar­rived, the cops nabbed him. Then they ex­torted money, threat­en­ing to tell his par­ents or his wife.
Sometimes, Doctor told Varma, they took the man in­side an ATM and emp­tied his ac­count. {#atm}
The man could do noth­ing. He had been made to feel what Varma called “al­most a pri­mal shame”, a shame con­structed by so­ci­ety and the state and then used to ex­tort money from him.

Varma wrote about it in a col­umn in *Mint*, and he does not blame a few rot­ten po­lice­men. “To me this is not a bunch of bad cops,” he said. “To me this is the in­cen­tives, this is the na­ture of the state.” {073-S01}
Why out­law some­thing that is nat­u­ral, vol­un­tary and in­fringes no one’s rights? Once the law went, he said, the Matunga racket was no longer pos­si­ble.
~ The same thing can hap­pen in any con­text. In a state with pro­hi­bi­tion, Varma said, po­lice can raid your house, find half a bot­tle of whiskey and drag you away, and that is mon­strous.
stories.why: Outlaw a vic­tim­less act and the state gets a ready-made lever of shame, which some­one will use to make money. Varma blames in­cen­tives, not in­di­vid­ual po­lice­men. Take away the law, and the lever goes with it. {#threeseventy}

pic.caption: Amit Varma on the Matunga racket

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on a case that tests the meaning of consent
stories.head: Dinner by mutual consent
body: In 2003, Amit Varma read about Armin Meiwes, a 42-year-old man in Rotenburg, Germany, whom his neigh­bours called nor­mal. From the time he was eight, he had fan­ta­sised about eat­ing a human being. {#eight}
He ad­ver­tised for a well-built young man who wanted to be eaten. Bernd Brandes an­swered, say­ing he had al­ways fan­ta­sised about being eaten, and con­sented at every stage, mostly on cam­era.

Brandes took twenty sleep­ing tablets and some schnapps. While he show­ered, Meiwes read a *Star Trek* novel. {#startrek} Then Meiwes killed him with a cleaver and ate the body over many days, with olive oil and gar­lic.

~ Cannibalism is not a crime in Germany; mur­der is. Is a man who con­sents to be eaten men­tally ill, and if so, is the killer in­sane too? “Who gets to de­fine san­ity and in­san­ity?” Varma asked. {073-S02}

quote.text: But there are many cases where it is not so clear cut and there is a con­tin­uum be­tween san­ity and in­san­ity.

stories.postscript: On the olive oil and gar­lic, Varma won­dered why there was no salt: “per­haps a human flesh has nat­u­ral salt like bacon does.” {073-J06}

pic.caption: Amit Varma on the German cannibal

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on a lobby, some studies and a guideline
stories.head: Fat framed, sugar walks free
body: In the show’s episode on re­vers­ing his di­a­betes, Amit Varma had laid out how sugar is the root of many bad things. Some even call Alzheimer’s type three di­a­betes. {073-J17}

Yet for decades, es­pe­cially in America, sugar was given a clean sheet and fat was de­monised. The sugar lobby spent heav­ily on re­searchers from Harvard and else­where, whose in­flu­en­tial stud­ies used bad method­ol­ogy and mis­took cor­re­la­tion for cau­sa­tion.

In 1977 the top di­etary body in the US is­sued guide­lines say­ing sugar was fine and fat was evil. Look at a chart of the obe­sity epi­demic, Varma said, and that is when it ex­plodes. {#guidelines}
~ His con­clu­sion was not to ban sugar. The state had stepped in be­liev­ing it would do good. “But its knowl­edge was not good enough.” {073-S03}
stories.why: State guid­ance can be cap­tured by a lobby and built on bad sci­ence, and be­cause ev­ery­one fol­lows it, the dam­age scales. Varma’s an­swer is not a ban but leav­ing the mat­ter to in­di­vid­u­als.

pic.caption: Amit Varma on the sugar lobby

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on what the casino taught him
stories.head: Never a rupee on roulette
body: Amit Varma played poker pro­fes­sion­ally for five years and spent a lot of time in casi­nos. Not once in all that time did he play a game against the house, or put a sin­gle rupee on a roulette table. {#roulette}
It is a los­ing propo­si­tion, he said. In a sense, stay­ing away was it­self a gam­ble: he had weighed the prob­a­bil­i­ties.

The ta­bles also showed him a darker side. He has seen gam­bling ad­dic­tion de­stroy lives, as drug and al­co­hol ad­dic­tion do, and when peo­ple close to him were caught by it, he tried to in­ter­vene and failed. {073-S05}
~ The state, he ar­gued, can do noth­ing here: so­cial prob­lems have to be solved by so­ci­ety. “The state should know its lim­its. If the state tries to step in, things be­come far worse.”

quote.text: In the case of peo­ple close to me, I have tried to make in­ter­ven­tions and I have failed be­cause ad­dic­tion is ad­dic­tion.

p4.credits: Everything is Everything was Amit Varma and Ajay Shah’s weekly show, 128 episodes from June 2023 to December 2025. This edition is made from Episode 73. The moving pictures, stills and chapter cards are from its video; the chapter art is by Simahina. Every play button starts the video at the moment it was said. The articles and headlines were written by Claude, an AI model, from the episode’s machine-made transcript, and checked against it. Other photographs are from Wikimedia Commons: John Locke (Godfrey Kneller, public domain); Vijay Kelkar (Press Information Bureau, Government of India, GODL-India). The covers on the shelf are from Amazon.

shelf.title: Alan Turing’s life and story
shelf.why: Ajay says study­ing Turing’s life ‘will re­shape your moral calculus’ by show­ing what state co­er­cion over pri­vate mat­ters ac­tu­ally costs.

shelf.title: Bootleggers and Baptists—The Education of a Regulatory Economist
shelf.creator: Bruce Yandle
shelf.why: Yandle’s ‘beau­ti­ful way of think­ing about how reg­u­la­tion works’: the moral cru­sader (the Baptist) and the black-market sup­plier (the boot­leg­ger) both want the ban, so they lobby for the same end, some­times with the boot­leg­ger fund­ing the Baptist.

shelf.title: Raees: An Empty Shell of a Gangster Film
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Amit’s re­view ar­gu­ing that the film gets pro­hi­bi­tion eco­nom­ics back­wards: a real boot­leg­ger would fund the anti-alcohol politi­cian, not fight him, be­cause their in­cen­tives are aligned.

shelf.title: Abby Philips Fights for Science and Medicine (Episode 310 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: A long de­fence of sci­en­tific medicine from liver doc­tor Abby Philips, on the ten­sion be­tween doing right by pa­tients and giv­ing them what they want.

shelf.title: How I Reversed My Type 2 Diabetes (Episode 9)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Amit’s ac­count of re­vers­ing his di­a­betes through diet: eat less ce­real, avoid pro­cessed food, and treat ghee as a su­per­food and sugar as poi­son.

shelf.title: Laws Against Victimless Crimes Should Be Scrapped (2008)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Amit’s case that ban­ning pros­ti­tu­tion, bet­ting and al­co­hol only hands these ac­tiv­i­ties to the un­der­world.

shelf.title: Why Is There A Commotion? (2017)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: One of Amit’s ear­lier pieces listed along­side the episode’s themes, for read­ers who want more of his writ­ing on them.

shelf.title: We Are All Gamblers (2010)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Amit’s ar­gu­ment that every life choice, from mar­riage to jobs to stocks, is a bet weighed on prob­a­bil­i­ties, so ‘gambler’ shouldn’t be an in­sult and sin­gling out gam­bling for stigma makes lit­tle sense.

shelf.title: The Dark Game (2014)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Amit has seen gam­bling ad­dic­tion de­stroy lives up close; his col­umns deal with that dark side hon­estly, with­out ask­ing for bans.

shelf.title: Aella on Twitter
shelf.creator: Aella
shelf.why: Aella is an openly happy sex worker who is also ‘in­cred­i­ble at data’ and runs large-scale sur­veys.

shelf.title: Knowingless
shelf.creator: Aella
shelf.why: Aella’s Substack, one of the few news­let­ters Amit pays for: strong data work on young people’s sex­ual lives from a for­mer sex worker who is also a very good data sci­en­tist, ‘so packed with insight’ about gen­der re­la­tions.

shelf.title: The Matunga Racket (2007)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: A con­crete case of how crim­i­nal­is­ing con­sent­ing adults turns a vic­tim­less ‘crime’ into a tool for po­lice ex­tor­tion.

shelf.title: Metrics of Empowerment (Episode 88 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Devika Kher, Nidhi Gupta and Hamsini Hariharan
shelf.why: Three schol­ars in­vent un­con­ven­tional, in­tu­itive mea­sures of women’s em­pow­er­ment, from who or­ders the gro­ceries to women in pris­ons and solo travel, along­side Amit’s own: ris­ing di­vorce rates.

shelf.title: We Should Celebrate Rising Divorce Rates (2008)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Amit’s provoca­tive ar­gu­ment that ris­ing di­vorce rates, often lamented as ‘be­com­ing like the West’, show more women gain­ing the agency and means to leave bad mar­riages.

shelf.title: Why Freedom Matters (Episode 10)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Despite the title, an eco­nomic his­tory of India told through the lens of free­dom: the boom after 1869, Nehru’s Fabian so­cial­ism, the lost years from the 1962 war to the Emergency, and the open­ing-up that lifted mil­lions out of poverty.

shelf.title: How to Do Development (Episode 57)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The case, built on Lant Pritchett’s ev­i­dence, that every human wel­fare in­di­ca­tor tracks per capita GDP, so sus­tained growth, not re­dis­tri­bu­tion or small solv­able projects, is the way out of poverty.

shelf.title: In Service of the Republic
shelf.creator: Vijay Kelkar and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The hosts’ frame­work for Indian eco­nomic pol­icy: when the state should step in, why its fail­ures cut across every do­main (HR, con­tract­ing, bud­get­ing, checks on co­er­cive power), and why the fix is checks and bal­ances and small, re­versible steps.

laughs.text: Amit on India’s old law against sui­cide: ‘It was the one crime for which you got pun­ished if you failed to com­mit it.’

Amit’s only time smok­ing up, circa 1995, in the back seat of a car with a friend and ‘a great world fa­mous gui­tarist I won’t name be­cause it’ll seem like too much of a hum­ble brag.’ The punch­line: ‘I felt noth­ing.’

Amit ex­plains ‘we are all gamblers’ using Pi, who had just been on Ajay’s lap. Putting him there was a bet: the chance he dis­rupts the shoot weighed against the joy and ‘the oxy­tocin flood­ing through you.’
Amit on im­port du­ties: ‘I buy some­thing in America, I bring it here, and I sell it to a friend. And im­me­di­ately it is a crime be­cause I haven’t paid the hafta to the state.’
Telling the can­ni­bal story, Amit notes the body was eaten with olive oil and gar­lic: ‘I don’t know why there was no salt, per­haps a human flesh has nat­u­ral salt like bacon does.’
Arguing for legal, reg­u­lated broth­els run by proper or­gan­i­sa­tions, Amit adds: ‘I don’t think HDFC or IDFC will do it, but you get what I’m say­ing.’
Amit on ‘whore’ as an in­sult: ‘Like which of us is not a whore in some way or the other if you use the term in that man­ner.’
Thoreau’s ‘lives of quiet des­per­a­tion,’ used for peo­ple who had to hide their sex­u­al­ity while it was crim­i­nalised.
Bruce Yandle’s ‘Bootleggers and Baptists,’ and how the Shah Rukh Khan film Raees got it back­wards by mak­ing the boot­leg­ger and the anti-alcohol politi­cian en­e­mies.

Definitions com­pared: the Oxford dic­tio­nary calls pros­ti­tu­tion ‘en­gag­ing in sex­ual ac­tiv­ity with some­one for pay­ment,’ while India’s Immoral Traffic Prevention Act calls it ‘the sex­ual ex­ploita­tion or abuse of per­sons for com­mer­cial pur­poses.’
Alzheimer’s being called ‘type three diabetes’ by some, men­tioned by Amit to show how many harms are traced back to sugar.
